paper_title: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.

The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand. 1. Introduction Human videos offer scalable source of training data for robot manipulation [23, 37, 72, 81] and egocentric world models [62, 68, 76]. Accurate metric 3D hand motion is essential for extracting high-quality supervision from these videos. Egocentric hand motion reconstruction aims to recover the 3D joint positions of both hands in camera coordinates. Detect-then-reconstruct methods [46, 48, 80] first localize hands and then estimate their 3D poses from image 1 crops. Within this paradigm, single-frame approaches lack temporal consistency, while motion-prior-based methods model temporal coherence but remain vulnerable to localization and tracking failures under occlusion. The current stateof-the-art methods ViDiHand [67] and ACE-Ego-Hand [35] instead adapt pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) to reconstruct hands directly from full-frame videos, eliminating the need for explicit hand detection and enabling recovery of occluded hand motion. However, both methods exhibit substantial errors in recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from in-the-wild videos [12], particularly in depth estimation and spatial localization, as Fig. 1 shows. key limitation is that directly regressing metric depth from appearance requires learning complex mapping that is highly sensitive to focal length and generalizes poorly to unseen cameras [47, 75], as illustrated in Fig. 2. Moreover, occlusion and hand truncation at image boundaries weaken the visual cues for hand localization, while coarse tokenization in both methods limits the preservation of fine-grained spatial details. Addressing these challenges further calls for richer spatial-temporal representations from VDMs and more consistent hand trajectory prediction over time. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, which reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into geometric constraint solving. Our key insight is that metric depth can be recovered by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joint predictions and the metric structure of MANO hands [51], both of which are more reliable than directly regressed depth. To realize this idea, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting (Sec. 3.2), which places each joint along its camera ray and constrains its depth using MANO joint distances. Unlike prior methods [20, 54, 63] that recover metric scale through bone-length fitting or 2D3D alignment, our approach exploits fine-grained constraints across multiple joints. We further introduce Clip-Level Ray Fitting to jointly estimate depth across video clip, leveraging temporal observations to constrain frames with unreliable joints. Accurate joint localization is essential for maintaining reliable geometric constraints, particularly under occlusion and truncation. In Sec. 3.3, we introduce the Joint-Heatmap Refiner to recover fine-grained joint positions using heat maps at eight times the resolution of the VDM token grid. To further handle ambiguous visual evidence, ConfidenceGated Fusion adaptively combines the refined 2D predictions with the fitted MANO hand, assigning greater weight to MANO estimates when joint localization is uncertain. We further enhance the VDM-based architecture with improved feature aggregation and temporal modeling in Sec. 3.4. The Multi-Level Latent Encoder aggregates features across all adapted VDM blocks to exploit multi-level representations. The Hand Latent Decoder decodes each Figure 2. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ViDiHand2. We consistently outperform existing methods on every metric. On in-the-wild data, ViDiHand2 reduces absolute joint error by over 40% compared with the strongest baseline. On in-domain benchmarks, it lowers the absolute and 2D joint errors of ACE-Ego-Hand by 20% and 31%. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify key limitation of existing VDM-based hand reconstruction methods: direct depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. To address this, we reformulate depth estimation as fine-grained geometric constraint solving, recovering metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned joint predictions and MANO hand structure. To support reliable geometric reconstruction, we introduce fine-grained joint localization and confidence-gated fusion for handling occlusion and truncation, along with multilevel feature aggregation and autoregressive rollout for stronger spatial-temporal modeling. We conduct extensive experiments on seven public datasets against 18 baselines. Evaluated on all ground-truth hands, ViDiHand2 ranks first on every metric of every dataset, both against their officially released weights and against the re-trained baselines, showing superior detection, 3D pose accuracy and smoothness. 2. Related Work 3D Hand Reconstruction. Detect-then-reconstruct methods regress MANO [51] parameters or mesh vertices from each detected hand crop [7, 33, 34, 39, 41, 44, 46, 48, 49, 52, 56, 70, 83]. Video methods aggregate crops over time [10, 32], learn motion priors [8, 21, 71, 74, 84] or estimate worldspace motion [50, 55, 66, 73, 77, 80]. Beyond pose and shape, the hand must also be placed in the camera frame. common practice is to regress camera translation alongside the hand under an assumed focal length [46, 48]. The fitting requires no hand crop, spans an entire video clip, and includes joints beyond the image boundaries. Parametric Models and Keypoints. Parametric models such as SMPL [36] and MANO [51] accumulate rotation errors along the kinematic chain. To avoid this, HybrIK [28], NIKI [29] and Minimal-Hand [82] derive the rotations from predicted 3D keypoints through inverse kinematics. MeTRAbs [54] uses the back-projected 2D location for joints inside the image and the root-relative 3D prediction for truncated ones. ViDiHand2 replaces this hard switch with learned gates that move the placed MANO hand toward the 2D locations according to their reliability. Diffusion Models for Perception. Recent work adapts pretrained diffusion models to correspondence, depth estimation, tracking and 3D perception [11, 14, 17, 19, 24, 42, 58, 60, 64, 78]. ViDiHand [67] and ACE-Ego-Hand [35] reconstruct hands from video diffusion features without hand detector, but both regress the hand depth. In monocular depth estimation and human mesh recovery, regressed metric depth is known to depend on the training cameras [30, 47, 75]. We aggregate the features of every block of pretrained VDM. Like ACE-Ego-Hand [35], we repurpose this VDM into deterministic, detector-free encoder. We apply the first 16 blocks of the Wan2.2 transformer [61], adapted with LoRA [16], to noise-free VAE latents without diffusion sampling. Each latent frame after the first covers four video frames. The transformer processes clip in chunks of 21 latent frames, whereas the fit of Sec. 3.2 spans the whole clip. The task tokens of each latent frame are two hand tokens, 42 joint tokens and four registers. In ACE-Ego-Hand, the same tokens enter separate decoder after the last adapted block and see only that blocks features. Our task tokens instead pass through every adapted block, where they use the block weights [65] and read the video tokens without changing them [26]. The hand tokens predict the MANO hand and the hand presence. The video tokens of the last block and ray encoding of form the feature map. Hand Latent Decoder. We decode the hand states and features of each latent frame into its video frames without fixed interpolation. Our temporal decoders build on the Wan VAE decoder [61] and also read latent frames of the adjacent chunks. In contrast, ACE-Ego-Hand linearly interpolates the hand states between latent frames. ViDiHand [67] adds learned residual to this interpolation. Autoregressive Rollout Adaptation. In the last four blocks of our transformer, each chunk also attends to the cached keys and values of the previous chunk [6, 69, 85]. ViDiHand instead processes each chunk independently, so the hand pose can jump at chunk boundaries. On autoregressive rollouts [18, 22], we train only bias on this attention. The supplement details chunked inference in Sec. D.8. 4. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Datasets. To test in the wild, on an unseen camera and scenes, we sample about one hour of Gen-HumanEgo [12], unused in training. Rule-based checks and visual inspection remove 3.79% of the frames of the seven datasets, mostly with inaccurate or missing labels or unusable images, as Sec. of the supplement details. Baselines. Fitting versus Regressing the Hand Depth. As Tab. 6 shows, fitting the hand depth transfers to an unseen camera far better than regressing it. head trained with the features to regress the depth reaches an in-the-wild MPJPE-abs-p of 81.24 mm, close to ACE-Ego-Hand and ViDiHand, and 42.52 mm for the depth over the focal length, whereas every fit stays at 38.83 mm or below. On the features trained with the depth head, the fit still reaches 32.55 mm, so the gap comes from how the depth is obtained, not from the features. Importance of Clip-Level Ray Fitting and Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting. Fitting over the clip smooths the motion, and the bone term, which ties the joints on their rays to the metric MANO joint-pair distances, improves the placement. One wrist trajectory per clip lowers the jitter of the per-frame fit from 3.39 to 1.26 mm/frame2 in-domain and from 3.65 to 1.61 mm/frame2 in the wild. Adding the bone term to the reprojection fit of MeTRAbs [54] and HandDGP [63] lowers its MPJPE-abs-p in the wild from 34.40 to 32.69 mm per frame and, over the clip, on every dataset by 0.17 to 1.73 mm. Importance of the Joint-Heatmap Refiner. In Tab. 7, the 2D locations of Sec. 3.3 have the largest in-domain effect of all designs, as their heat maps are eight times finer than the feature map. Using only the coarse token-attention locations, as ACE-Ego-Hand does, is smoother but less accurate and raises the MPJPE-abs-p from 19.62 to 32.30 mm in-domain and from 32.59 to 39.71 mm in the wild. Keeping only those inside the image gives 20.20 mm in-domain. Confidence-Gated Fusion versus Either Source. In Tab. 8, whose rows share one model and one wrist trajectory and differ only in the output joints, the fusion is more accurate than either of its sources on every accuracy metric in both settings. It combines the MANO hand, which is complete but need not align with the image, with the 2D locations, which align with the image but are unreliable under occlusion and beyond the border. In-domain, it thus lowers the EPE2D-p of the MANO hand by 7%, from 5.03 to 4.67 px, and its MPJPE-p from 9.75 to 9.50 mm. The learned gate is also more accurate and smoother than setting the gate to the confidence, gj = cj. Section of the supplement defines all variants and reports more metrics. 5. Conclusion We propose ViDiHand2, which reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from regression into geometric constraint solving. Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and ClipLevel Ray Fitting compute the depth of clip on the rays of the test camera, the Joint-Heatmap Refiner and ConfidenceGated Fusion handle occlusion and truncation, and the MultiLevel Latent Encoder, Hand Latent Decoder and Autoregressive Rollout Adaptation improve accuracy and smoothness. ViDiHand2 substantially outperforms 18 methods on every metric, in-domain and in the wild, at 57 FPS, enabling scalable hand motion data collection for embodied AI. Limitations. ViDiHand2 needs the camera intrinsics, which egocentric devices provide in practice. It also runs offline, which suits recorded videos but not closed-loop control. 8 Acknowledgements. sections.content: This supplement gives the datasets and the evaluation protocol in Sec. A, quantitative results in Sec. B, more qualitative results in Sec. and implementation details in Sec. D, which cover every module of Sec. 3: the Multi-Level Latent Encoder, the Joint-Heatmap Refiner, Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting with Clip-Level Ray Fitting, the Hand Latent Decoder, the Autoregressive Rollout Adaptation and Confidence-Gated Fusion. The variants of the ablation studies and the runtime follow in Secs. and F. References such as Tab. 1 or Eq. (2) point to the main paper.

A.5. Metrics The frame accuracy FAcc is the fraction of test frames with neither false positive nor detection failure. F1 is the harmonic mean of the precision and the recall of the detections, with the counts pooled over all hands of dataset. False positives enter FAcc and F1 only. MPJPE-abs is the joint error in camera coordinates, MPJPE the joint error after subtracting the wrist of each hand, and PA-MPJPE the joint error after aligning scale, rotation and translation. Each is the mean over the 21 joints of hand, also of joints outside the image, and then over the hands. EPE2D is the pixel distance between the predicted joints, projected with the ground-truth intrinsics, and the ground-truth joints, over the visible ground-truth joints, with each distance capped at the image diagonal. The suffix -p denotes that an error is computed over all visible ground-truth hands. Each detected hand is evaluated with the matched prediction, and each detection failure receives penalty. For MPJPE-abs-p, MPJPE-p and EPE2D-p, the penalty is the error of default prediction. This default prediction places the MANO mean hand of the same handedness with the wrist at depth of 0.5 on the camera ray through the image center. Since PA-MPJPE aligns each prediction to the ground truth, the default prediction can obtain lower error than an actual one. The penalty of PA-p is therefore the root-mean-square distance of the ground-truth joints from their centroid, an upper bound on the Procrustes-aligned error of any non-degenerate prediction. Jitter is the mean acceleration Xt+1,j 2Xt,j + Xt1,j of the predicted joints Xt,j of method in camera coordinates, in mm/frame2, over every three consecutive frames in which the hand is detected. It has no penalty and no ground-truth term, so it measures smoothness and not accuracy. In the comparisons on hands detected by all methods, hand-frame is kept when every method detects it, the errors have no penalty, and Jitter uses the triplets of consecutive kept frames. Implementation Details D.1. Multi-Level Latent Encoder The frozen Wan2.2 VAE encodes the whole clip once as one latent stream. As in ACE-Ego-Hand [15], the first 16 of the 30 blocks of the Wan2.2-Fun-5B-Control transformer [26] process the noise-free latents of each chunk without diffusion sampling. LoRA [9] adapts the attention and feed-forward layers of these blocks, and the pretrained weights remain frozen. Each latent frame also carries 48 task tokens for the two hands, the 42 joints and four registers. ACE-Ego-Hand uses the same tokens but reads them from the output of the last block with separate decoder. In ViDiHand2, the task tokens instead pass through every adapted block with the weights of that block. Within block, the task tokens attend to the video tokens of that block and to all task tokens of the chunk. The video tokens attend only to each other, over the whole chunk in space and time, so the task tokens do not change the video features. When the task tokens attend to the video tokens, the video keys keep only the rotary encoding of time. Training ViDiHand2 is trained in the two stages of Tab. S23 on the six in-domain training splits of Tab. S1, starting from the released Wan2.2 weights. The training chunks of 21 latent frames come from one causal latent stream per clip, as at inference, and every frame contributes to the losses. Speed augmentation subsamples 60% of the chunks by 2 or 3 with equal probability. The fit keeps the original frame rate, so these chunks show faster hand motion than the recordings. We also paste black occluders into 25% and other hands into 20% of the chunks and low-pass filter 30% of the chunks. Clips with the smallest and the largest hands are sampled twice as often. Both stages use AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.999) and total batch size of eight chunks on 8 A100 GPUs, and gradients are clipped at norm of 1.0. The first stage trains the LoRA adapters, the task tokens, the heads, the decoders and the gates for 50k steps, with learning rate of 2104 for the heads and 104 for LoRA after warm-up of 200 steps. The second stage trains the cache bias for 3k steps on autoregressive rollouts. ViDiHand2 has 3.0B parameters, of which 107.5M are trained. The LoRA adapters and the trained patch convolution hold 86.6M of them, the task-token adapters 2.4M and the heads 18.5M, including the 3.8M of the decoders and the 0.23M of the part gates. Inference The first chunk covers 81 frames and every later chunk the next 84, so every chunk holds 21 latent frames. clip that does not end on latent boundary is padded by repeating the last frame, and the padded frames are dropped from the output. The chunks are processed autoregressively, and from block 12 on, the transformer of each chunk attends to the cached keys and values of the previous chunk. When the cache is used, blocks 12 to 15 run twice, once with and once without the cache. The pass with the cache provides the task-token states for the pose. The pass without the cache provides the video features and the states for the shape and the presence. The decoders of each chunk also read the last two latent frames of the previous chunk and the first latent frame of the next. The chunks do not overlap, but their decoded spans do, and the decoded features of the overlap are averaged. After the last chunk, clip-level pass takes the median of the per-frame shapes of each hand and adds the clip-wide shape residual. It then applies MANO and the Clip-Level Ray Fitting to the whole clip. Equation (7) then blends the two estimates of each joint with the learned gate, and Eq. (S7) moves the MANO hand onto the blend to give the output joints. The hand presence confidence threshold is 0.05.
